lesson.title: Disaccharides: When Two Sugars Become Something New
lesson.summary: Disaccharides form when two monosaccharides join through a condensation reaction, and familiar examples like sucrose, lactose, and maltose show how the identity and orientation of the linking bond changes a sugar's taste, source, and digestibility.
lesson.body:
A disaccharide forms the moment two monosaccharides react and join together, and the chemistry behind that joining is a condensation reaction, the same dehydration synthesis that builds every biological polymer. The hydroxyl group on the anomeric carbon of one sugar reacts with a hydroxyl group on a second sugar, water is released, and a new covalent linkage called a glycosidic bond holds the two sugar rings together. Because that anomeric carbon can be in either the alpha or the beta configuration, and because it can bond to any of several available hydroxyl groups on the second sugar, the exact same two monosaccharides can in principle link in more than one way, producing molecules with different shapes and different biological fates.

Three disaccharides come up constantly in biology and nutrition, and each one illustrates the point. Sucrose, ordinary table sugar, is built from one glucose and one fructose joined through their anomeric carbons in an alpha, beta 1,2 linkage. Plants synthesize sucrose specifically because it is a stable, non reducing sugar that can be pumped through vascular tissue from the leaves where it is made to roots, fruits, and growing tips where it is needed. Lactose, the sugar found in milk, is built from one galactose and one glucose joined by a beta 1,4 glycosidic bond. Digesting lactose requires the enzyme lactase, and people who lose lactase activity after childhood, which is common worldwide, become lactose intolerant because undigested lactose passes into the large intestine where bacteria ferment it, producing gas and drawing in water. Maltose, sometimes called malt sugar, is built from two glucose units joined by an alpha 1,4 glycosidic bond, and it appears whenever starch is partially broken down, for example during digestion or when grain is malted to brew beer.

Notice that the same monomer building block, glucose, appears in both maltose and, as you will see in the next section, the giant polysaccharide starch, and the exact same alpha 1,4 bond links glucose units in both cases. This is not a coincidence: maltose is essentially a two unit fragment of starch, produced as an intermediate when the enzyme amylase chews through a starch chain. Comparing maltose's alpha 1,4 bond to lactose's beta 1,4 bond also previews an idea explored in depth later, that the alpha or beta orientation of a glycosidic bond, not just which sugars are involved, is what determines which enzyme can recognize and cleave it. Human digestive enzymes are built to cleave alpha bonds efficiently, which is why we can digest maltose and sucrose but cannot digest structural beta linked carbohydrates like cellulose.

Breaking a disaccharide back down into its two component monosaccharides requires hydrolysis, the reverse of condensation, in which a water molecule is added across the glycosidic bond. This is exactly what happens in your small intestine: enzymes such as sucrase, lactase, and maltase are specific hydrolytic enzymes, each shaped to recognize one particular disaccharide and split it into absorbable monosaccharides. Without that hydrolysis step, disaccharides are generally too large and too specifically shaped to cross the intestinal lining intact, so digestion is not optional, it is the mechanism that makes the sugar in your food usable at all.
